newsitem.title: POLAND: POPE ENDING 11-DAY TRIP THAT CHALLENGED POLES.
newsitem.headline: POPE ENDING 11-DAY TRIP THAT CHALLENGED POLES.

text.p: The long pilgrimage home ending on Tuesday has deeply touched 77-year-old Pope John Paul and challenged Poles to ponder how they should use the freedoms he helped them to win.

The Pontiff arrived late on Monday to spend a night in a monastery in the south-eastern hill town of Dukla, once home to a 15th century Franciscan brother called Jan whom he was to make a saint at a mass in nearby Krosno the following morning.
He was then scheduled to return to the city of Krakow for an airport farewell ceremony, before flying to Rome at the end of the demanding 11-day journey.

The last leg of the trip through 12 towns and cities took him to the southern highlands near his birthplace of Wadowice, and to Krakow where he rose from student to Cardinal and which he left in 1978 for his unexpected election as Pope.
In Krakow, the Pope experienced some of the most emotional moments of a voyage studded with memories.

On Monday he prayed in silence there at the grave of his mother, father and brother whose loss before he was 21 hurt him deeply. The previous evening, visiting his Krakow Alma Mater, he recalled the terrible day in 1939 when wartime Nazi German occupiers took almost 150 professors to a concentration camp.
The Pope has attracted crowds estimated by the Church at around six million -- evidence of the great influence he enjoys in his mostly Catholic homeland.
The biggest gathering was a mass in Krakow on Sunday when he told about 1.5 million compatriots they should use freedoms won with the 1989 fall of communism to spread love and truth.

How Poles should make use of their liberty, which the Pope helped them to gain through his support of the then Soviet bloc's first free trade union Solidarity, has been a thread running through his words during the trip.
The Pope insisted that freedom was meaningless if not shaped by moral values.

"When there is a void in the area of values -- when chaos and confusion reign in the moral sphere -- freedom dies, man is reduced from freedom to slavery, becoming a slave to passions and pseudo-values," he said during a mass near the start.
On June 3 in Gniezno, where the presidents of seven nations gathered to hear him, the Pope also warned of an invisible new wall of "economic and political selfishness" dividing Europe.
He said no countries should be excluded from communities now arising on the continent and stated "There will be no European unity unless it is based on unity of the spirit."
Nowhere did the Pope challenge current Polish values more strongly than over the law, introduced last year, allowing abortion in cases of a woman's financial or other hardship.

He said societies allowing abortion were barbarous, no matter what their other achievements. On Monday he praised doctors and nurses who refused to conduct the procedure the Roman Catholic Church views as the killing of children.

These and other comments addressed highly political matters as campaigning gets underway for parliamentary elections due in September that will pit pro-Catholic and anti-abortion rightist opposition parties against the ruling ex-communists.
Although rightist groups gathered around Solidarity hope the impact of the visit will help bring them victory, even the ex-communists paid tribute to the effects of his presence.

"I expressed my...gratitude to the Pope for the fact that there is an atmosphere of calm, which we need so much, during his pilgrimage," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said after meeting John Paul on Sunday.
